text: 3 Analysis of Weighted Contrastive Learning
3.1 Unified formulation of weighted Contrastive Learning losses
Problem setup.

The goal of representation learning Bengio et al. (2013) is to learn a mapping [MATH f:\mathcal{X}\rightarrow\mathcal{Z}] from input data [MATH X=(x_{i})_{i\in[1..n]}\in\mathcal{X}^{n}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n\times p}] such that its representation [MATH Z=(z_{i})_{i\in[1..n]}:=f(X)\in\mathcal{Z}^{n}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}] retains useful information for a variety of downstream tasks.

Given a similarity matrix [MATH W=(w_{ij})\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}] such that [MATH w_{ij}\geq 0] for [MATH i\neq j] , and [MATH S=(s_{ij})] where [MATH s_{ij}=s(z_{i},z_{j})=s(f(x_{i}),f(x_{j}))] for [MATH s:\mathbb{R}^{q}\times\mathbb{R}^{q}\to\mathbb{R}] some measure of similarity in the latent space, the weighted InfoNCE loss is defined as

[MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}:=- rac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j
eq i} rac{w_{ij}}{\sum_{k

Remark. Originally, SupCon, [MATH y] -Aware and [MATH \mathbb{X}] -CLR all define the InfoNCE loss in terms of several augmentations of every given sample. We argue this case can be recovered from the above formulation by concatenating several data augmentations in a single matrix [MATH X] .
Let us we recall the weighting schemes that correspond to several well-known frameworks:
SupCon Khosla et al. (2020): [MATH w_{ij}=1] if [MATH y_{i}=y_{j}] and 0 otherwise for a labeled dataset [MATH (X,Y)] with [MATH Y\in[1..C]^{n}] and [MATH C] the number of classes.
y-Aware Dufumier et al. (2021): [MATH w_{ij}=\exp{\left(-\|y_{i}-y_{j}\|^{2}\right)}] for a weakly-labeled dataset [MATH (X,Y)] with [MATH Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times\ell}] the meta-data.

[MATH \mathbb{X}] -CLR Sobal et al. (2024): [MATH w_{ij}=\exp(\cos(y_{i},y_{j})/\tau^{\prime})] for an image-caption dataset [MATH (X,Y)] with [MATH Y] the textual descriptions of the images encoded by a pretrained text encoder.
In each of the above cases, similarity in the latent space is measured with cosine similarity: [MATH s_{ij}=\cos(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau] , with [MATH \tau] a temperature hyperparameter.
The similarity function [MATH s] and similarity matrix [MATH W] are symmetric, so [MATH s_{ij}=s_{ji}] and [MATH w_{ij}=w_{ji}] for all [MATH i,j\in[1..n]] .

We divide the analysis into two parts. First, we study the soft weighting regime, where [MATH W] is strictly positive (§ 3.2–3.6). We then turn to the hard or sparse regime, where [MATH W] may contain zeros (§ 3.7–3.8).
3.2 Entropic lower bound
Under a strict-positiveness assumption, we can state the entropic lower bound of the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss (proof in Appendix A):

Under Assumption 3.2 and assuming [MATH w_{ij}>0] for [MATH i\neq j] , viewing the weighted InfoNCE loss [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] as a function of [MATH S=(s_{ij})] over the space of symmetric similarity matrices, the global minimum is attained precisely when
[MATH s_{ij}^{*}=\log(w_{ij})+c\qquad\text{for}\ i\neq j]
for some constant [MATH c\in\mathbb{R}] . Moreover, that minimum equals

[MATH \min_{S}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}=- rac{1}{n}\sum_{i
eq j} rac{w_{ij}}{\sum_{k
eq i}w_{ik}}\log\left( rac{w_{ij}}{\sum_{k
eq i}w_{ik}}ight).] (1)

This result echoes what has been previously obtained using a probabilistic framework Poole et al. (2019), with [MATH s] being the “critic” discriminating positive pairs against negative ones. In our case, we obtain a geometric characterization of [MATH Z^{*}] which is more precise than previous works11 1 In Poole et al. (2019), the constant [MATH c] depends on [MATH i] . (in part thanks to Assumption 3.2) and which does not depend on a dichotomy between positive and negative samples as in the classical view of contrastive learning.
3.3 Connection with the Distance Geometry Problem
We can now express the relationship between the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss and the Distance Geometry Problem (DGP) Liberti et al. (2014) as immediate corollaries of Theorem 3.3:

When latent similarity is given by [MATH s_{ij}=-\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|^{2}] and [MATH w_{ij}=\exp(-d_{ij})] for a symmetric dissimilarity matrix [MATH D=(d_{ij})] , attaining the entropic lower bound of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] stated in Theorem 3.3 amounts to solving the DGP
[MATH \|z_{i}^{*}-z_{j}^{*}\|^{2}=d_{ij}+c\qquad\textrm{for }i\neq j,] (2)
for any constant [MATH c\in\mathbb{R}] .

When [MATH s_{ij}=\cos(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau] and [MATH w_{ij}=\exp(-{d_{ij}})] for a symmetric dissimilarity matrix [MATH D=(d_{ij})] , attaining the entropic lower bound of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] amounts to solving the cosine problem
[MATH \cos(z_{i},z_{j})=-\tau d_{ij}+c^{\prime}\qquad\textrm{for }i\neq j,] (3)
for any constant [MATH c^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}] .

These corollaries show that minimizing [MATH w] -InfoNCE amounts to finding a low-dimensional embedding with prescribed similarity, up to an additive constant [MATH c] or [MATH c^{\prime}] . We will go on to show that a mild condition on [MATH n] and [MATH \rank(D)] suffice to entail that [MATH c=0] or [MATH c^{\prime}=1] .
3.4 Existence and uniqueness of the optimal embedding

Having established the link between DGP and weighted InfoNCE, we ask ourselves the question of existence and uniqueness of solutions to these two families of problems. The answers involve a classical notion from computational geometry Alfakih and others (2018).
(EDM) An [MATH n\times n] matrix [MATH D=(d_{ij})] is called an Euclidean Distance Matrix (EDM) if there exist points [MATH z_{1}^{*},\dots,z_{n}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{q}] such that

We call the points [MATH z_{1}^{*},\ldots,z^{*}_{n}] a [MATH q] -dimensional realization of [MATH D] . The embedding dimension is defined as the smallest dimension [MATH r] of a Euclidean realization, or equivalently as the dimension of the affine span of any given Euclidean realization. Distinct Euclidean realizations of an EDM in a given dimension are congruent, i.e. they differ by a Euclidean isometry. A minimal Euclidean realization (i.e. in [MATH \mathbb{R}^{r}] ) is called a set of generating points of [MATH D] . Finally, we say that [MATH D] is spherical if those generating points can be chosen such that [MATH \|z_{1}\|=\cdots=\|z_{n}\|=\rho] for some radius [MATH \rho>0] . The smallest such [MATH \rho] is called the radius of a spherical EDM.

Assume that the number of points [MATH n] is strictly greater than [MATH 2q+3] . Assume that [MATH s_{ij}=\exp(-\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|^{2})] and [MATH W=(\exp(-d_{ij}))] for [MATH D=(d_{ij})] an [MATH n\times n] dissimilarity matrix with [MATH \rank(D)\leq q+2] . Then the entropic lower bound of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] is attained iff [MATH D] is EDM of embedding dimension [MATH r\leq q] , up to diagonal elements. In that case, the minimum [MATH Z^{*}] satisfies [MATH \|z^{*}_{i}-z^{*}_{j}\|=d_{ij}] for all [MATH i,j\in[1..n]] and is essentially unique (i.e. up to Euclidean isometry).

Next, we consider the case of Corollary 3.5 where the similarity metric between latent vectors is given by cosine similarity. This is the most common use-case in CL Khosla et al. (2020); Dufumier et al. (2021); Sobal et al. (2024) and it has a rigidity property analogous to Theorem 3.7, which we prove in Appendix B.2:

Assume that [MATH n>2q+4] . Assume that [MATH s_{ij}=\exp(\cos(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau)] and [MATH w_{ij}=\exp(-d_{ij})] for [MATH D=(d_{ij})] an [MATH n\times n] dissimilarity matrix with [MATH \rank(D)\leq q+1] . Then the entropic lower bound of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] is attained by some embedding [MATH Z^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}] iff [MATH D] is a spherical EDM (up to diagonal elements) with embedding dimension [MATH r\leq q] and radius [MATH \rho\leq 1/\sqrt{2\tau}] (with equality when [MATH r=q] ). In that case, [MATH \cos(z_{i},z_{j})=1-\tau d_{ij}] for all [MATH i,j\in[1..n]] and [MATH Z^{*}] is essentially unique (i.e. the normalized vectors [MATH \widetilde{z}_{i}:=z_{i}^{*}/\|z_{i}^{*}\|] are unique up to linear Euclidean isometry).
3.5 Supervised classification: Soft SupCon
We now show that the Soft SupCon weighting scheme arises as a direct application of Theorem 3.8.

Let [MATH y_{i}\in[1..C]] be one of [MATH C] discrete classes associated with each sample and define [MATH w_{ij}=1] if [MATH y_{i}=y_{j}] and [MATH w_{ij}=\varepsilon\in(0,1)] otherwise. Assume [MATH n>2q+4] and consider [MATH s_{ij}=\exp(\cos(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau)] . If [MATH C\leq q] and [MATH \tau\leq(C-1)/(-C\log\varepsilon)] , then the entropic lower bound of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] is attained by some [MATH Z^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times q}] , which is unique up to linear Euclidean isometry of the normalized embeddings. At the optimum, one has [MATH \cos(z_{i},z_{j})=1] when [MATH y_{i}=y_{j}] , and [MATH \cos(z_{i},z_{j})=1+\tau\log\varepsilon] otherwise. In particular, all points from the same class collapse to a single representation, and the [MATH C] classes form a simplex with uniform inter-class similarity [MATH \beta=1+\tau\log\varepsilon] . The simplex is regular when [MATH \tau^{*}=(C-1)/(-C\log\varepsilon)] , corresponding to [MATH \beta^{*}=-1/(C-1)] .
3.6 Supervised multivariate regression

Next, we state three results corresponding to various weighting schemes that can be encountered when using continuously labeled data (see Appendix C.1 for the proofs). Let [MATH (X,Y)] be a labeled dataset with [MATH \ell] continuous labels [MATH Y\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times\ell}] . We assume throughout that [MATH n>2q+4] so that Theorem 3.7 and 3.8 can be applied. Our first result concerns the case where Euclidean distance is used as a dissimilarity function in both label space and representation space.

Assume [MATH \ell\leq q] . If [MATH w_{ij}=\exp({-\|y_{i}-y_{j}\|^{2}})] and [MATH s_{ij}=-\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|^{2}] , the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss attains its entropic lower bound in [MATH Z^{*}=(\widetilde{y}_{i})_{i=1}^{n}] , where [MATH \widetilde{y}_{i}=(y_{i},0,\dots,0)\in\mathbb{R}^{q}] for [MATH i\in[1..n]] , which is essentially unique.
Our next result is a negative one and concerns the Euclidean–spherical [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss, i.e. the [MATH y] -Aware loss Dufumier et al. (2021).

Even if [MATH \ell\leq q] , the [MATH y] -Aware InfoNCE loss, which is the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss with [MATH s_{ij}=\cos(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau] and [MATH w_{ij}=\exp(-\|y_{i}-y_{j}\|^{2})] , does not attain the entropic lower bound unless the [MATH y_{i}] happen to lie on a hypersphere in [MATH \mathbb{R}^{\ell}] .
On the other hand, the spherical–spherical case, as in the [MATH \mathbb{X}] -CLR loss Sobal et al. (2024), does attain the entropic lower bound and offers a spherical counterpart to Theorem 3.10.

If [MATH \ell<q] and [MATH \tau\leq\tau^{\prime}] , the [MATH \mathbb{X}] -CLR loss Sobal et al. (2024), which is the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss with [MATH s_{ij}=\cos(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau] and [MATH w_{ij}=\exp(\cos(y_{i},y_{j})/\tau^{\prime})] attains the entropic lower bound in the points [MATH z_{i}^{*}=(y_{i}/\|y_{i}\|,\sqrt{\tau^{\prime}/\tau-1},0,\dots,0)] for [MATH i\in[1..n]] . Moreover, that minimum is essentially unique.

In practice Sobal et al. (2024), the dimension of text embeddings in [MATH \mathbb{X}] -CLR is [MATH \ell=768] for CLIP and the latent dimension [MATH q=2048] for ResNet50. It was also found that [MATH \tau^{\prime}\approx\tau] gives the best classification accuracy on ImageNet.

Practical implications. Theorem 3.11 and 3.12 suggest that the pair of similarity functions used to define [MATH (W,S)] should be chosen consistently to allow for a realizable optimum. The spherical–spherical or Euclidean-Euclidean weighting schemes are therefore preferable over the Euclidean–spherical scheme (as in [MATH y] -Aware).
3.7 Sparse weights and limiting properties

The assumption of positive weights, i.e. [MATH w_{ij}>0] in Theorem 3.3, may be relaxed to [MATH w_{ij}\geq 0] assuming that [MATH \sum_{ik}w_{ik}>0] so that [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] is well defined: we term this the sparse case. Although any sparse matrix [MATH W] can be understood as a limit of a sequence of positive matrices [MATH (W_{m})] , the optimum of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W}] need not be the limit of the optimum of [MATH \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{NCE}}^{W_{m}}] because in general convergence is not uniform. Moreover, the configuration of points which attain the minimum may behave qualitatively different in the limit.

In Appendix D.1 we prove that in the sparse case, the entropic lower bound continues to hold and that it is sharp. We give a necessary and sufficient for it to be optimal (i.e. impossible to improve upon). We go on to show that it is optimal in the case of the so-called Euclidean SupCon (i.e. the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss with a hard SupCon weighting scheme and Euclidean similarities [MATH s_{ij}=-\|z_{i}-z_{j}\|^{2}] ) but that quasi-optima can be produced in any number of qualitatively distinct configurations. This comes in stark contrast to the soft case where optima are essentially unique (Theorem 3.7).
3.8 SupCon

We now consider the case of SupCon proper (i.e. the [MATH w] -InfoNCE loss with a hard SupCon weighting scheme and spherical similarities [MATH s_{ij}=\cos(z_{i},z_{j})/\tau] ). Using a compactness argument, we see in Appendix D.2 that the entropic lower bound is sub-optimal. We go on to prove the following theorem:
Let [MATH C] denote the number of discrete classes and [MATH \ell_{c}] the size of the [MATH c] th class. Assume that [MATH C\leq q] .
The SupCon loss has a unique global minimum over the matrices of the form [MATH G/\tau] , with [MATH G] an [MATH n\times n] cosine matrix.
That minimum has collapsed representations and can be expressed in terms of class prototypes [MATH \mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{C}\in\mathbb{S}^{q-1}] which are unique up to linear Euclidean isometry.
If [MATH c\neq c^{\prime}] , the value of [MATH \cos(\mu_{c},\mu_{c^{\prime}})] depends only on [MATH (\ell_{c},\ell_{c^{\prime}})] .

In particular we see that SupCon suffers from representation collapse which generalizes both Nguyen et al. (2024) and Behnia and Thrampoulidis (2024) in that we make no assumptions on [MATH \tau>0] nor do we require an infinite number of samples.

In the case of balanced classes, we easily recover the result from Graf et al. (2021) that SupCon optima correspond to regular simplices (Appendix D.2, Theorem D.6). Moreover, Hard and Soft SupCon have similar optima: both collapse classes and yield uniform inter-class similarities. For Hard SupCon, [MATH \beta_{\mathrm{hard}}=-1/(C-1)] depends on [MATH C] ; for Soft SupCon, [MATH \beta_{\mathrm{soft}}=1+\tau\log\varepsilon] depends on [MATH (\tau,\varepsilon)] but not on [MATH C] . Choosing [MATH \tau^{*}=(C-1)/(-C\log\varepsilon)] yields a regular simplex.
This equivalence breaks under class imbalance: SupCon produces non-uniform inter-class similarities, grouping minority classes more closely, whereas Soft SupCon is agnostic to class imbalance.
